note: Evergreen places. These do not expire, but opening hours and prices change — the card links out so you can check before you travel. Distances are estimated from the République / Canal Saint-Martin area.

items.title: Du Pain et des Idées
items.transit: Walk — it is essentially your local
items.why: One of the two or three best bakeries in Paris and it is a six-minute walk from your door. Get the pain des amis and the escargot pistache-chocolat. Critical detail: it is closed at weekends, so this is a weekday-morning mission, not a Saturday one. The 1889 painted-glass ceiling is worth looking up at while you queue.

items.title: Ten Belles
items.area: 10 rue de la Grange aux Belles
items.why: The café that started Paris's specialty coffee scene, still one of the best, and it is around the corner from you. Tiny inside — get your cup and take it to the canal, which is 90 seconds away. Their sister bakery Ten Belles Bread in the 11th does excellent sourdough.

items.title: Holybelly 5 & 19
items.why: The pancakes-with-a-fried-egg breakfast that made rue Lucien Sampaix a destination. No reservations, so go at opening or expect to queue — which, since it is a seven-minute walk, is a much smaller problem for you than for everyone else in the queue.

items.title: Boulangerie Utopie
items.why: Award-winning bakers who cannot leave well enough alone — squid-ink baguettes, matcha croissants, seasonal pastries that change constantly. Where Du Pain et des Idées is classical perfection, this is the experimental one. Worth doing both in a single Saturday morning and comparing.

items.title: Mamiche
items.why: Come for the babka. Two women running a loud, cheerful bakery that is the opposite of the hushed reverence of French pâtisserie. Their chocolate babka sells out — go before noon on a weekend.

items.title: Café Oberkampf
items.why: The shakshuka is the thing, and the banana bread is the other thing. Small, sunny, vegetarian-friendly, and the sort of place you end up going back to every month. Weekday mornings are calm; weekends mean a wait.

items.title: Brûlerie de Belleville
items.why: An actual working roastery rather than a café that sells beans. They open to the public for cuppings and tastings — you can taste four coffees side by side and finally understand what people mean by 'notes of'. Check the day before, as public hours are limited.

items.title: Boot Café
items.why: A former cobbler's shop the size of a garden shed, with the original blue 'CORDONNERIE' facade kept intact. Three seats. Genuinely excellent coffee. It is the most photographed café door in Paris and still somehow not annoying.

items.title: Marché d'Aligre + Marché Beauvau
items.times: Tue–Sun mornings, closed Monday · best before 12:00
items.why: The best market in Paris, and not a close contest. Three things in one square: the covered Beauvau hall with the serious cheese and meat traders, the open-air produce market where the prices are shouted and negotiable, and a small daily flea market where people sell genuinely odd second-hand things. Go Sunday morning, buy lunch, eat it in the Coulée verte fifteen minutes away.

items.title: Marché des Enfants Rouges
items.why: The oldest covered market in Paris, running since 1615, now mostly food stalls where you eat at communal tables — Moroccan, Japanese, Italian, and an excellent vegetarian traiteur. Arrive before 12:30 on a weekend or you will not get a seat. Combine with the design shops on rue de Bretagne and rue Charlot.

items.title: Marché Saint-Quentin
items.transit: Walk, or M4/M5 to Gare de l'Est
items.why: Your own covered market — a big 1866 iron-and-glass hall ten minutes away that most people in the 10th walk past without going in. Excellent fishmonger, a very good Italian counter, and a bar in the middle where you can have a glass of wine at 11am with no judgement whatsoever.

items.title: Puces de Vanves Flea Market
items.times: Sat & Sun, 07:00–14:00 — it really does end at 14:00
items.why: The flea market to go to if you actually want to buy something. Saint-Ouen is bigger and more famous but has become expensive and antique-dealer-serious; Vanves is people selling from trestle tables and you can haggle. Silver cutlery, old linens, ceramics, prints. Go at 8am — by noon the good things are gone.

items.title: Puces de Saint-Ouen
items.times: Sat–Mon · Marché Paul Bert Serpette is the one to head for
items.why: The largest antiques market on earth, and it is genuinely overwhelming, so go with a plan: walk straight to Marché Paul Bert Serpette for 20th-century furniture and design, and Marché Dauphine for prints and curiosities. Ignore the tat near the Metro exit — the real market starts after you cross under the périphérique.

items.title: La Trésorerie
items.why: If you want to make your flat nicer, start here — it is a ten-minute walk away and it is the best homewares shop in Paris. A former treasury building filled with well-made European household objects: enamel, linen, brooms, kitchen tools, paint. There is a Scandinavian café inside. Go on a Saturday morning, then walk to Mamiche.

items.title: Empreintes
items.why: Four floors of contemporary French craft — ceramics, glass, metalwork, jewellery — run by the national crafts guild, so everything in it is made by a working French artisan. It functions as a free museum you happen to be allowed to buy from. The ceramics floor is exceptional.

items.title: E. Dehillerin
items.why: Open since 1820, unchanged since about 1900, and still where professional chefs buy their copper. Bare wooden floors, stock piled to the ceiling, handwritten price tags, staff who will find you exactly the right whisk out of four hundred. Buy one good copper pan and you will have it for life. Julia Child shopped here.

items.title: Artazart
items.transit: Walk — it is on the canal
items.why: A design and photography bookshop sitting directly on the Canal Saint-Martin, five minutes from you. Orange shopfront. Excellent for graphic design, architecture and photobooks, and a very good place to find a present. Combine with a coffee and a walk along the water.

items.title: Ofr. Bookshop
items.why: A cramped, brilliant art-book and magazine shop in the north Marais with a tiny gallery at the back and a courtyard. This is where you find the independent magazine you did not know existed. Around the corner from the Marché des Enfants Rouges — do both.

items.title: Green Factory
items.why: Plant shop specialising in closed terrariums — sealed glass ecosystems that water themselves and last for years. They run workshops where you build your own, which is a genuinely good two-person activity for a rainy Saturday and you leave with something for the flat.

items.title: Magasin Sennelier
items.why: An art supply shop on the Seine since 1887. Cézanne and Degas bought pigments here; Sennelier invented the oil pastel for Picasso. Pigments in glass jars floor to ceiling. Even if you do not paint, it is one of the most beautiful shop interiors in Paris and it costs nothing to walk in.

items.title: Musée de la Chasse et de la Nature
items.why: The strangest good museum in Paris. Two hôtels particuliers stuffed with taxidermy, hunting weaponry and contemporary art installed among them without explanation — a room with an owl in the ceiling watching you, a cabinet of invented creatures. It is funny, unsettling and completely unlike anywhere else. If you only visit one small museum, make it this.
items.imageSubject: Musée de la chasse et de la nature

items.title: Pavillon de l'Arsenal
items.why: A free museum entirely about Paris itself — how the city was built, how it is being rebuilt, what is planned for the next twenty years. There is a giant interactive model of the whole city on the ground floor. If you want to understand the place you live rather than just look at it, this is the single best two hours available, and it costs nothing.

items.title: Musée Carnavalet
items.why: The history of Paris, in a Marais mansion, free forever. Proust's actual bedroom, Napoleon's things, shop signs from streets that no longer exist, and a beautiful garden courtyard to sit in. It reopened after a long renovation and is now one of the best-designed museums in the city. Free means you can drop in for forty minutes without guilt.

items.title: Petit Palais
items.why: A free art museum with a semicircular interior garden and a café in it, opposite the Grand Palais. Courbet, Monet, Rembrandt, and almost nobody in the rooms because everyone queues across the road instead. The garden café is one of the nicest cheap sit-downs in central Paris.

items.title: Musée de la Vie Romantique
items.why: A green-shuttered house at the end of a cobbled lane where George Sand and Chopin's circle spent their evenings, kept as it was. The point is the garden café — roses, a glass conservatory, tea and cake, and the fact that you cannot hear the city at all. It is the most romantic free thing in Paris.

items.title: 59 Rivoli
items.why: A former bank taken over by artists in 1999, later legalised by the city, now six floors of working studios you can walk straight into. You climb a spiral staircase past thirty artists actually painting and can talk to any of them. Free, chaotic, and about as far from a white-cube gallery as it gets.

items.title: Parc des Buttes-Chaumont
items.transit: M5 to Laumière, or M7bis to Buttes-Chaumont
items.why: The best park in Paris and it is fifteen minutes from you. Built on an old gypsum quarry, so instead of the flat symmetry of French gardens you get cliffs, a suspension bridge, a lake and a temple on a rock with a view over the whole north of the city. Sunday afternoons the lawns fill with people doing nothing. Rosa Bonheur inside is a good open-air bar.

items.title: Parc de Belleville
items.why: The best free sunset view in Paris, and hardly anyone goes. A terrace at the top of a steep hill looking straight down over the whole city with the Eiffel Tower on the right. Sacré-Cœur has the same view, a hundred times the crowd and someone trying to sell you a bracelet. Bring a bottle, arrive forty minutes before sunset.

items.title: Coulée verte René-Dumont
items.transit: M8 to Bastille, start behind the Opéra
items.why: A 4.5 km garden built on a disused railway viaduct, running east from Bastille four metres above the street. It came twenty years before New York's High Line and is much less crowded. You walk through rose arches at first-floor window height, looking into people's flats. Under the arches at the Bastille end are craft workshops in the Viaduc des Arts.

items.title: La Petite Ceinture
items.transit: Varies by section — the 15th and 20th sections are the best
items.why: The abandoned railway that once ringed Paris, closed in 1934 and slowly reclaimed by trees and foxes. Several stretches are now legally open to walk. It is overgrown, silent, covered in graffiti and feels like you have found a gap in the city. The 15th section is the longest and easiest; the 20th section near Père-Lachaise is the wildest.

items.title: The Covered Passages
items.area: 2nd and 9th — Panoramas, Jouffroy, Verdeau, Vivienne, Grand-Cerf
items.why: Glass-roofed shopping arcades from the 1800s, the ancestors of the shopping mall, of which about eighteen survive. This is the single best thing to do in Paris when it rains, because you are under glass almost the whole way. Chain them: Panoramas, then across the boulevard to Jouffroy, then Verdeau, then walk to Galerie Vivienne, which is the beautiful one. Second-hand bookshops, stamp dealers, an old cane shop, tea rooms.

items.title: Passage Brady
items.transit: Walk, or M4 to Château d'Eau
items.why: Your own covered passage, and completely unlike the elegant ones near the Bourse — this one has been Little India since the 1970s, wall to wall with Indian, Pakistani and Bangladeshi restaurants and grocers under a glass roof. Cheap, chaotic, excellent for vegetarian food, and eight minutes from your flat. The grocers at the Faubourg Saint-Denis end are the best-stocked in central Paris.

items.title: Quartier de la Mouzaïa
items.why: A grid of cobbled private lanes behind Buttes-Chaumont, lined with two-storey houses covered in roses and wisteria, built cheaply in the 1900s because the old gypsum mines underneath meant nothing heavy could go on top. You will not believe you are still in Paris. It is twenty minutes from you and almost nobody knows it exists. Combine with the park.

items.title: La Butte-aux-Cailles
items.transit: M7 direct to Place d'Italie or Corvisart
items.why: A hilltop village inside the 13th that the city never flattened — cobbles, low houses, ivy, murals, and a lively cheap bar scene at night. Also here: the Piscine de la Butte-aux-Cailles, a 1920s art deco swimming pool fed by an artesian well, still open to the public for about €4. Nearby is the Cité Florale, five tiny streets named after flowers. The 13th is the arrondissement people from the 10th most reliably neglect.

items.title: Cimetière du Père-Lachaise
items.transit: M2 to Père Lachaise, or M3 to Gambetta and walk downhill
items.why: 44 hectares of cobbled lanes under old chestnut trees — a park that happens to be a cemetery, and one of the quietest places in eastern Paris. Enter at the top (Gambetta) and walk down, which saves you the hill. Chopin, Wilde, Piaf, Proust. Go on a weekday morning when it is empty and misty.

items.title: Jardin Villemin
items.why: Your nearest proper green space — a walled garden behind the canal with a lawn you are allowed to sit on, a community vegetable plot and considerably fewer people than the canal bank on a sunny evening. Good for a coffee-and-a-book hour when you do not want a plan.

items.title: Croissant & Baguette Classes — La Cuisine Paris
items.why: Croissant-making, baguette-making, macarons and market-to-table classes taught in English on the Seine. The croissant class is the one to do: three hours of laminating dough, and you finally understand why a good one costs what it costs. Book a fortnight ahead for weekend slots.

items.title: Make Your Own Perfume — Le Studio des Parfums
items.why: You sit at an organ of raw perfume materials with a perfumer and blend a bottle you take home, with the formula kept on file so you can reorder it. It is a genuinely unusual two-person afternoon and a much better anniversary idea than dinner. Book ahead.

items.title: Wine Tasting — Ô Chateau
items.why: A proper tasting in a 17th-century cellar, run in English by qualified sommeliers, aimed at people who want to stop guessing in wine shops. The introduction-to-French-wine session covers the six main regions in two hours and is the fastest way to make every future dinner better.

items.title: Pottery & Ceramics Workshops
items.transit: M5 to Oberkampf / M9 to Voltaire
items.why: The 11th and 20th are full of small ceramics ateliers running two- and three-hour wheel-throwing tasters for pairs, and you keep whatever you make once it is fired. It is the best rainy-Saturday activity in Paris: you are inside, you are using your hands, and the flat ends up with something you made. Search 'atelier céramique cours débutant Paris 11' and book the one with a free weekend slot.

items.title: The Tamil Quarter, La Chapelle
items.area: Rue Cail, rue Perdonnet, rue Louis-Blanc
items.transit: Walk, or M2 to La Chapelle
items.why: Twelve minutes from your flat is the largest South Asian quarter in France — Tamil and Sri Lankan grocers, sari shops, sweet counters and some of the best and cheapest food in Paris. Rue Cail is the spine of it. At the top is Sri Manicka Vinayakar Alayam, the biggest Hindu temple in the country, tucked into a side street off rue Pajol. Worth knowing simply because it is close, and because most guides to Paris behave as if it does not exist.

items.title: Musée Guimet
items.priceNote: ~€13 · free on the first Sunday of the month
items.why: The national museum of Asian art, and its Indian and Himalayan collections are among the best outside Asia — Gandhara sculpture, Chola bronzes, a rotunda library that looks like a film set. It also programmes Indian classical music and dance in its auditorium through the season, which is the most reliable place in Paris to hear a proper sitar or Bharatanatyam performance. Check the auditorium listings, not just the galleries.

items.title: Bouillon Julien
items.why: An 1906 art nouveau dining room — peacock murals, mahogany, glass flowers — serving classic French food at prices that have not caught up with the decor. Bouillons were built to feed workers cheaply and this one still does. Eight minutes from your flat. No reservations for small tables, so go at 19:00 or after 21:30.

pairings.text: Le Syndicat is four minutes further up the street

items.title: Urfa Dürüm
items.why: A Kurdish grill the size of a corridor where one man has been making lahmacun and dürüm over charcoal for twenty years. Bread rolled and cooked in front of you, herbs, sumac onions, no cutlery. Around nine euros and consistently one of the best things you can eat in this city at any price. Queue is normal.

pairings.text: Passage Brady is three minutes south
Le Verre Volé for a glass after

items.title: Le Petit Cambodge
items.why: Cambodian bo bun and steaming bowls, six minutes away on the corner by the canal. Fresh, herby, quick, and reliably good on a night when neither of you wants to decide anything. It is also part of the neighbourhood’s memory — the terrace was attacked in 2015 and reopening it was a deliberate act. Nobody makes a thing of it; you should just know.

pairings.text: The canal is thirty seconds away
Point Éphémère, ten minutes up the water

items.title: Clamato
items.why: The seafood annexe of Septime, and the only way most people ever get to eat that kitchen’s cooking — Septime books out months ahead, Clamato takes no reservations at all. Oysters, small plates, natural wine. Turn up when it opens or eat late. Worth the wait in a way that very few no-booking places are.

pairings.text: La Buvette for one more glass after

items.title: Dong Huong
items.why: A Vietnamese canteen in Belleville that has been feeding the neighbourhood for decades — strip lighting, formica, enormous bowls of pho and bun bo hue for about twelve euros. No atmosphere whatsoever and that is the point. Go with the crowd at lunch, then walk up the hill to the park.

pairings.text: Parc de Belleville sunset, ten minutes uphill

items.title: Le Potager du Marais
items.why: Entirely vegetarian, and — unusually for Paris — cooking actual French dishes rather than salads: bourguignon, blanquette, tartiflette, all done without meat. Tiny, about twenty covers, so book. Useful to have in your pocket, because vegetarian French food is much harder to find here than vegetarian international food.

pairings.text: Musée de la Chasse is four minutes away

items.title: Chez Alain Miam Miam
items.why: A man in the oldest covered market in Paris making one thing — an enormous galette-wrapped sandwich, assembled slowly and theatrically while you wait, with comté, avocado, herbs and chilli. The queue is long because he refuses to hurry. Go at 11:30 before the market fills, eat it standing at the counter.

pairings.text: You are already in the Marché des Enfants Rouges

items.title: Gonflé
items.transit: Walk — behind Saint-Vincent-de-Paul, near Gare du Nord
items.why: Timothy Breton cooked at the Plaza Athénée and Le Bristol and then opened a bakery on a quiet street behind Saint-Vincent-de-Paul, which tells you most of what you need to know about how the pastry is made. The charcoal croissant filled with vanilla cream is the one everyone photographs; the kouign-amann is the one to actually order. Ten minutes from home and worth the detour past the closer options.

pairings.text: Coffee at Ten Belles, ten minutes back down
Eat it in Square Cavaillé-Coll opposite the church
